content: The erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), also known as the sedimentation rate, sed rate, or Biernacki Reaction, is a non-specific and indirect measure of acute-phase reactant concentrations, which are altered in inflammatory conditions. It is commonly used as a medical screening test. To perform the ESR test, anticoagulated blood is placed in an upright tube, referred to as a Westergren tube. The rate at which red blood cells (RBCs) settle to the bottom of the tube is measured and reported in millimeters per hour (mm/hr). In the presence of inflammation, elevated fibrinogen levels in the blood cause RBCs to adhere to one another, forming stacks called rouleaux. These rouleaux settle more rapidly. Rouleaux formation can also occur in certain lymphoproliferative disorders where high levels of immunoglobulins are secreted. However, rouleaux formation is a physiological finding in some animal species, such as horses, cats, and pigs. The baseline ESR is slightly higher in females compared to males and increases with age. ESR values are influenced by the size, shape, and number of RBCs, as well as other blood components like immunoglobulins. ESR levels are elevated in conditions such as pregnancy, anemia, and any cause of inflammation. Conversely, ESR is decreased in conditions like sickle cell anemia, polycythemia, and congestive heart failure. The ESR test was first developed in 1897 by Polish physician Edmund Biernacki. In 1918, Swedish pathologist Robert Sanno Fåhræus and Alf Vilhelm Albertsson Westergren further refined the test, which is now commonly referred to as the Fåhræus-Westergren test or simply the Westergren test. This method uses sodium citrate-anticoagulated blood specimens. Although ESR is frequently ordered, it is not a highly effective screening test. It is primarily useful for diagnosing three specific conditions: multiple myeloma, temporal arteritis, and polymyalgia rheumatica, where ESR values may exceed 100 mm/hr. It is also used in the differential diagnosis of Kawasaki disease and may be elevated in chronic infectious conditions such as tuberculosis and infective endocarditis. Additionally, ESR is a component of the Pediatric Crohn’s Disease Activity Index (PCDAI), which assesses the severity of inflammatory bowel disease in children. The clinical utility of ESR is limited to monitoring therapeutic responses in certain inflammatory diseases, such as temporal arteritis, polymyalgia rheumatica, and rheumatoid arthritis. It can also serve as a crude measure of disease activity in Hodgkin’s lymphoma and is used to define adverse prognostic factors in the staging of this condition. However, ESR has low sensitivity and specificity as a screening test in asymptomatic individuals. An elevated ESR without other clinical findings should not prompt extensive laboratory or radiographic evaluations. Normal ESR values are reported in millimeters per hour (mm/hr). These values are generally higher in individuals with anemia and in Black populations. For adults, reference ranges can be calculated using formulas based on age and gender. For children, normal ESR values are as follows: Newborns: 0 to 2 mm/hr. Neonates to puberty: 3 to 13 mm/hr (or 0 to 15 mm/hr in some references).
